solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One in a canoe at sea where islands abound

indicators.note: 'One' is placed inside the letters of 'a canoe' before they are rearranged
something at sea is adrift and all over the place, so the canoe's letters get jumbled

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A lone paddler out on the open water in a canoe, somewhere in a scattered island chain.
explanation.walkthrough: Put I into A CANOE and shake the lot up to get OCEANIA; the canoe and the islands both sit happily in the Pacific picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Oceania is the Pacific region made up of thousands of islands, from Polynesia to Melanesia.

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters spanning the poet's name and the next word

blocks.note: the last letter of the poet's name plus the first two of the following word

explanation.surface: A reader enjoying the poetry of Ariosto, the Italian Renaissance poet of Orlando Furioso.
explanation.walkthrough: ariostO DElights holds ODE across the word break; naming a real poet makes the hiding place feel like plain literary chat.
explanation.definitionFit: An ode is a lyric poem, so a piece of poetry written in lines.

clue.text: Flat-bottomed vessels in Devon river region

indicators.note: the vessels are placed inside the name of the Devon river

blocks.note: the Exe flows through Devon to Exeter
pans are shallow flat-based cooking vessels

explanation.surface: Barges or punts moored on a river somewhere in the county of Devon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat-bottomed vessels' suggests punts or barges on the river, but they are kitchen cookware.
explanation.definitionFit: An expanse is a wide open area of land or sea, close enough to a stretch of territory.

clue.text: Beat up a Liberal in an old province

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' means the word reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to thrash them
used as is
the standard abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: Colonial-era violence: a Liberal politician roughed up in some former province of the empire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat up' reads as one phrase meaning assault, but 'up' is separate and turns TAN over.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal was a province of South Africa until 1994, when it became KwaZulu-Natal.

clue.text: Attendant needing coal yet to be moved

indicators.note: the letters of 'coal yet' still have to be shifted into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A servant whose coal delivery has arrived but has not yet been shifted to the cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: COAL plus YET rearranged gives ACOLYTE.
explanation.definitionFit: An acolyte assists a priest at the altar, and more loosely is any follower or helper.

clue.text: Bellow beginning to race with paddle

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only the start of 'race' is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
an oar is a paddle for rowing

explanation.surface: A coxswain shouting as a rowing race starts and the crews pick up their paddles.
explanation.walkthrough: R from race plus OAR; 'with' simply joins the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: To bellow and to roar are synonyms, both meaning to shout loudly and deeply.

indicators.note: to overthrow something is to topple it, so in a down clue the pieces are turned upside down

blocks.note: the indefinite article, shortened
a tsar was the Russian emperor

explanation.surface: A follower of Haile Selassie, the Ethiopian emperor, somehow toppling an emperor himself.
explanation.walkthrough: A TSAR turned over reads RASTA. The surface is neatly ironic: Rastafarians revere Selassie as an emperor rather than overthrow one.
explanation.definitionFit: Rastafarians venerate Haile Selassie I, the last emperor of Ethiopia, as a divine figure.

blocks.note: surface reading: a paperknife, the blade used to slit envelopes
setter's reading: the person who opens a letter, namely whoever it was sent to

explanation.walkthrough: The obvious answer is a knife, but the question mark invites the literal sense: the person entitled to open the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The person named on an envelope is its intended recipient, and normally the one who opens it.

indicators.note: the warehouse keeps the sulphur, holding it within its walls

blocks.note: a depot is a storage building
the chemical symbol for sulphur

explanation.surface: A tyrant stockpiling sulphur, perhaps for gunpowder, in a store of his own.
explanation.walkthrough: S goes inside DEPOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is an absolute ruler with unchecked power, which is what a dictator is.

clue.text: Vicious perhaps to stop one being supportive

indicators.note: to stop a hole is to plug it, so the name fills the middle of 'one'

blocks.note: taken as written
Sid Vicious was the Sex Pistols' bassist; 'perhaps' marks a first name defined by example

explanation.surface: Someone cruel trying to block a friend from offering help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vicious' reads as an adjective, but it is the surname of punk musician Sid Vicious, supplying SID to plug into ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: To be onside is to be in agreement and backing someone, a British colloquial usage.

clue.text: For cheese we need Sally churning

indicators.note: churning stirs milk vigorously, so the letters of the phrase are stirred up

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A dairy needs Sally at the butter churn to make its cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: The churn is a genuine dairy image, so the anagram indicator hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Wensleydale is a crumbly white cheese from the Yorkshire Dales, a specific example of the category.

blocks.note: spotlessly clean, pure white
a hall is a large country mansion

explanation.surface: Ministers meeting in some immaculate stately home.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the London street is being read as a literal 'white hall'.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitehall is the London street lined with ministries, used by metonymy for the British civil service and state.

indicators.note: 'say' tells us to speak the word, so we use its pronunciation not its spelling

blocks.note: to purchase is to buy, which is pronounced like the prefix bi-
ceps are porcini mushrooms

explanation.surface: A shopping list: pick up some mushrooms as part of a muscle-building diet.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first word is sounded out; CEPS is the French name for the prized mushrooms that Italians call porcini.
explanation.definitionFit: The biceps is the large muscle at the front of the upper arm.

indicators.note: wrangling is quarrelling or struggling, and the letters of 'clash or' are wrestled into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Faculty politics: a donnish dispute or argument in the common room.
explanation.walkthrough: Wranglers are also top Cambridge maths graduates, so the indicator fits the academic surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholar is a learned person engaged in study, a close synonym of an academic.

clue.text: Last of intake failing to pass

indicators.note: only the final letter of 'intake' is wanted

blocks.note: the closing letter of the word
a lapse is a slip or failure

explanation.surface: The weakest student in the year group is failing to get a pass mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' wants to be an exam result, but it is a verb, as time passes.
explanation.definitionFit: Time elapses when it goes by, so to elapse is to slip by or go past.

indicators.note: the word for trouble comes after the phrase 'an enormous' in the answer

blocks.note: the indefinite article, shortened
a straightforward synonym
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: Some huge problem dogging a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a girl's name; 'girl' in a clue often points to a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Abigail is a female given name, and dated slang for a lady's maid.

clue.text: The plane designed in East like Jumbo?

indicators.note: something designed has been worked into a new shape, so the letters of 'the plane' are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter
taken as written
the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A jumbo jet built somewhere in the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumbo' suggests the Boeing 747, but it is Jumbo the famous Victorian elephant; the question mark marks the switch.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephantine means huge and lumbering, resembling an elephant, and Jumbo was a celebrated circus elephant.

indicators.note: the answer is contained within the letters of the phrase that follows

blocks.note: straddles the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: An instruction to an athlete or horse to compete in the following event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' looks like the verb of the surface, but it is a cricket noun. In cricket an extra is a run not scored off the bat, such as a wide or a bye.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket scoring, extras are runs credited to the batting side without the batter hitting the ball.

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so the word's sound matters rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a mounted soldier of the Middle Ages, with a silent first letter

explanation.surface: A herald declaring that an old soldier is stepping down from service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retire' suggests leaving work, but here it means going to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is when people go to bed, and to retire is an old-fashioned way of saying go to bed.

blocks.note: a car is a road vehicle
Tel is a short, pet form of the name Terry

explanation.surface: A phone call coming from young Terry's car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' reads as a phone call, but it means a group of colluders, as in a drugs ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartel is a group of firms or criminals acting together to control a market, which is a ring.

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for good
Maurice Ravel, the French composer of Boléro

explanation.surface: A fine musician playing in the Rolling Stones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Stones' looks like the rock band; the question mark allows a literal reading, a mass of small stones.
explanation.definitionFit: Gravel is a loose collection of small rounded pebbles, stones taken together as a mass.

indicators.note: to embody is to take in within one's body, so the monarch holds 'a'

blocks.note: Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's cipher
used as is

explanation.surface: A king or queen who is also a gifted musician.
explanation.walkthrough: A goes inside ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Having an ear for music means a natural talent for pitch and melody.

clue.text: Female by meadow in little jumper

indicators.note: 'by' means next to, so the two parts sit side by side

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for female
lea is a poetic word for a meadow

explanation.surface: A woman standing by a field wearing a small sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is the British word for a sweater, which is the false trail; here it is something that jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: A flea is a tiny insect famed for leaping great distances relative to its size.

blocks.note: to rattle someone is to unsettle them
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A serpent that has disturbed a ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an anagram or reversal instruction, but it simply means rattle.
explanation.definitionFit: Rattler is the informal American name for the rattlesnake, a venomous pit viper.
